title: AI-Assisted Code Comprehension & Debugging
description: AI-assisted code comprehension and debugging practice for /prep: debug a seeded-bug codebase with an AI helper under a time box, learn techniques (repro-first, hypothesis prompting, bisecting, verifying AI output), and keep a playbook of techniques. Invoked by the prep orchestrator via --aidebug, --ai, --comprehension.
scope_in: The skill of fixing unfamiliar code fast and correctly while using an AI assistant: framing context, hypothesis-driven prompting, reproducing first, localising (bisect, tracing, logging), reading unfamiliar code, verifying and critiquing AI suggestions, minimal test-driven fixes, regression guarding, time management; runnable Python codebases with seeded bugs.
scope_out: Algorithm puzzles (prep-dsa), building features from scratch, model/prompt-engineering theory, non-debugging code review style, languages other than Python for the practice repos.

modes.output: one verified runnable repo with seeded bugs; fix it in the time box using the AI helper; hidden tests grade it
short lesson (when/why/how, anti-pattern) plus a 5-minute drill on a tiny repo that forces that technique
an AI-style diagnosis or patch for a repo, partly wrong; you decide what to trust and prove it with tests
spaced repetition: a fresh repo for techniques or bug classes you missed
interview simulation: terse interviewer, AI helper allowed, no hints, process and result both scored

ladder: One file, one bug, a failing test names it: off-by-one, wrong operator, swapped arguments. 15 min.
3-5 files, one bug whose symptom is one call away from the cause: wrong unit, bad default, missed None case. 20 min.
6-8 files, two independent bugs, misleading symptoms: mutable default argument, aliasing, stale cache, sort stability. The helper may be wrong. 30 min.
Multi-module, three bugs where one masks another: timezone/rounding, encoding, cache invalidation, ordering assumptions, retry/idempotency logic. 40 min.
Realistic service, 10+ files, four interacting bugs plus a suspicious-looking but correct red herring and a plausible wrong AI claim; a naive fix breaks hidden tests. 50 min.

flaws.F-AI-NO-REPRO: Asked the AI or edited code before reproducing the failure and reading the test output.
flaws.F-AI-VAGUE-PROMPT: Prompt lacked the failing test, error text, expected vs actual, or relevant code; got a generic answer.
flaws.F-AI-CONTEXT-DUMP: Pasted the whole repo or logs without narrowing; noise drowned the signal.
flaws.F-AI-NO-HYPOTHESIS: Changed things without a stated, falsifiable hypothesis about the cause.
flaws.F-AI-BLIND-TRUST: Applied or believed an AI suggestion without verifying it with a test, run or code read (including falling for a planted wrong claim).
flaws.F-AI-SYMPTOM-FIX: Patched the symptom (special-case, try/except, test-shaped hack) instead of the root cause.
flaws.F-AI-SHOTGUN-EDIT: Made several unrelated edits at once so the effect of each was unknowable.
flaws.F-AI-OVERSCOPE: Rewrote or refactored far beyond the bug; diff much larger than needed.
flaws.F-AI-REGRESSION: Fix broke a previously passing test or behaviour.
flaws.F-AI-TEST-TAMPER: Edited or weakened tests to make them pass.
flaws.F-AI-NO-VERIFY: Declared done without rerunning the test suite after the last change.
flaws.F-AI-STOPPED-EARLY: Fixed some bugs and stopped; remaining hidden failures were never searched for.
flaws.F-AI-TIME-MISMANAGEMENT: Spent most of the time box on one dead end or on reading before running anything.

x_fields.bugs_total: Number of seeded bugs in the repo.
x_fields.bugs_fixed: Number fixed at the final submission.
x_fields.tests_failed_first_run: How many public tests failed on the first run, and whether the user ran them before editing.
x_fields.first_repro_s: Seconds until the user first reproduced the failure.
x_fields.ai_prompts: Number of times the user consulted the AI helper.
x_fields.prompt_quality: 1-3: 1 vague, 2 has the symptom, 3 has the symptom, a hypothesis and the minimal context.
x_fields.ai_trap_outcome: caught | fell | not-triggered | not-applicable (planted wrong AI claim).
x_fields.techniques_used: Technique names the user actually applied (matches the playbook).
x_fields.techniques_new: Techniques or methodologies new to the playbook this session.
x_fields.strategy: One sentence: order of steps the user followed.
x_fields.diff_lines: Changed lines in the user's fix.
x_fields.reference_diff_lines: Changed lines in the reference fix, for the minimal-diff comparison.
x_fields.regressions: Public or hidden tests that passed before and failed after the user's change.
x_fields.time_s_to_first_fix: Seconds until the first bug was fixed.
x_fields.variant: Review mode only: how the repo differs from the original.

items_note: the whole repo dir: repo/ (buggy), fixed/ (reference), tests_public/, tests_hidden/, meta.json, plus the user's final tree
rubric_body:
Score the process and the result separately.

**Result (from the harness):** bugs fixed / total, regressions, test tampering, diff size vs reference.

**Process (from the transcript, all must-haves):**
- Reproduced first: ran the tests and read the failure before editing or prompting.
- Prompts carried the symptom, the evidence and a hypothesis; context was narrowed, not dumped.
- Each AI claim was verified (run, test, or code read) before it became an edit.
- One change at a time, re-running tests after each; diff close to the reference.
- Kept going after the first green public test: looked for the remaining bugs.

Nice-to-have: wrote a regression test, stated a root cause in one sentence, used bisect/logging/debugger deliberately.
outcome_rule:
- **pass**: all bugs fixed (hidden tests green), no regression, no test tampering, within the time box, and at most one of F-AI-BLIND-TRUST / F-AI-NO-REPRO.
- **partial**: more than half of the bugs fixed, OR all fixed but over time, with regressions or a major process flaw.
- **fail**: half or fewer fixed, tests tampered with, or gave up.
gate_extra: Harness is mandatory: `python3 harness/judge.py verify <dir>` must exit 0 before the repo is shown. It proves, with the Python stdlib only: the buggy tree fails the public and hidden tests; the reference tree passes everything; each seeded bug, applied alone to the fixed tree, makes at least one hidden test fail; and no hidden test fails for a bug that is not listed. `python3 harness/judge.py selftest` proves the harness itself.

Seeded bugs must be realistic, one root cause each, and described in `meta.json` as a patch (file, buggy snippet, fixed snippet, bug class, technique that exposes it). Public tests must expose at least one bug; hidden tests must cover all of them plus regression behaviour.

Planted AI traps (levels 3+) are fixed in `meta.json` in advance: a plausible claim, why it is wrong, and the test that proves it. The user is told up front that the helper can be wrong; the trap is revealed in the debrief, never earlier.
Dedupe: skip any `item.ref` already in memory (`MEM seen aidebug <ref>`) unless in review mode; refs follow `aidebug-<bugclass>-<slug>`.
Ground truth for every claim the helper makes comes from running the code, not from reading it.
loop_extra:
### aidebug specifics
All paths relative to this skill's directory. Work in the scratchpad: `P=<scratchpad>/aidebug/<ref>`. `MEM` as above; `PB` = `python3 scripts/playbook.py` (the technique ledger, see below).

**Technique ledger (the point of this skill).** `PB` keeps `playbook.md` in the memory dir (`$(MEM path aidebug)/playbook.md`, never capped): every technique or methodology the user learned or invented, with a name, a one-line how/when, the evidence (item ref + date), and status `taught` / `tried` / `owned` (owned = used correctly unprompted in 2 sessions). Before any session: `PB show` (what they already own; do not re-teach it). At Remember: `PB add "<name>" --how "<one line>" --when "<trigger>" --ref <item ref> --status taught|tried|owned [--origin user|skill]`; `--origin user` for something the user invented or adapted; re-adding a name updates it and its status instead of duplicating. `PB catalog` lists the curated techniques in `references/techniques.md` that are not yet in the playbook.

**Generate (debug/mock/review)** — write `$P/{repo/,fixed/,tests_public/,tests_hidden/,meta.json}` per `harness/judge.py` docstring: a small realistic Python app (inventory, billing, rate limiter, scheduler, parser, cache layer...) with clear module boundaries, a `README.md` of 5-10 lines, and a `run_tests.sh`-free layout (`python3 -m unittest`). Seed bugs by editing a correct tree (`fixed/`) into `repo/`; record every bug in `meta.json`. Level = number of bugs, file count, how far the symptom is from the cause, masking, red herrings, traps (see ladder).
**Verify** — `python3 harness/judge.py verify $P`. Exit 0 required; on failure read `stage`/`detail`, fix, retry (max 3), else tell the user and pick another repo.
**Present** — copy `repo/` and `tests_public/` to `<workdir>/aidebug-work/` (the user's working tree; tell them the path), print the README, the test command (`python3 -m unittest discover -s tests_public -v`, run from that folder), the time box (L1 15m, L2 20m, L3 30m, L4 40m, L5 50m; `mock` as given), the rules, and that `/prep` can be asked as the AI helper. Never show `fixed/`, `tests_hidden/` or `meta.json`.
**Interact — AI helper protocol.** The user may ask the helper anything, prefixed `ask:` (or in plain words). Log each consultation (time, prompt summary, quality 1-3). Answer like a competent but fallible coding assistant: use only what was actually pasted or described plus what the helper can read in the working tree when asked; give hypotheses, not the fix, unless the user explicitly asks for a patch. At level 3+ the helper may deliver the planted trap from `meta.json` when the user asks the relevant question; otherwise it stays accurate. Never reveal hidden tests, `meta.json` or the reference. If asked to just fix it, comply but tag the item with the F-AI-BLIND-TRUST risk and make the user verify. Hints use the shared tiers (1 nudge, 2 pattern/where to look, 3 skeleton, 4 patch) and cost outcome as the rubric says.
**Submit** — when the user says done (or time ends): `python3 harness/judge.py judge $P <workdir>/aidebug-work` returns per-bug status, public/hidden results, regressions, test tampering, diff size, flaws. Report counts and the first failing hidden test name plus its message; do NOT reveal the reference.
**Debrief** — per bug: root cause, the technique that exposes it, whether the user got it. Reveal the trap and how it could have been caught. Show diff vs reference. Map process flaws from the transcript to taxonomy codes and `x` fields.
**Remember** — `save-item` the whole `$P` (not `__pycache__`), `append` one episode with `x`, then ledger updates via `PB add` for every technique used, taught or invented (one call each), and at most 3 `MEM note` lines.

**learn mode** — pick the user's weakest technique (profile tags, else the first not in the playbook per `PB catalog`). Teach in ≤12 lines from `references/techniques.md`: when to use, how, an anti-pattern, an example prompt (bad vs good). Then a 5-minute drill on a tiny verified repo (level 1-2) that is only fixable efficiently using that technique. Record it as `--status taught`; it becomes `tried` after a correct use, `owned` after correct unprompted use in 2 sessions.
**critique mode** — present a repo, a failing symptom and an AI-written diagnosis plus patch where some claims are false (kept in `meta.json`). The user must decide which claims to accept and prove each verdict by running something. Graded on claims correctly accepted/rejected with evidence, not on speed.
**mock mode** — no hints, interviewer tone, helper allowed but not coached, ask 'walk me through your approach' at the start and 'what would you do differently' at the end; both score process and result.
output_format: Terse. Repo path and rules first, nothing else. The helper answers briefly and says what it is unsure about. Debrief ≤10 lines. Code in fenced blocks. No praise padding.
